chapter: Gangsters, records, women musicians and the blues
title: Arriving known by her records; "Downhearted Blues" and piano rolls
summary: New Yorkers knew her from Paramount records; "Downhearted Blues" was the first blues to sell 100 percent mechanical and also appeared on piano rolls for which she was paid.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: What was your -- now, did anyone know you in New York when you came to New York? I mean, you were known in Chicago, obviously.
No.
But not in New York.
They just knew me by my records, that's all.
Oh, you had already started making records.
Oh, I had made records for Paramount.
I see.
I had made -- yes, I made records for Paramount. And I think I made records for Bennett Jeanette.
Right.
Yes.
So you weren't exactly an unknown when you --

No, I was well known, because I was in fact what you call -- well, what people call famous, from my records. Because if you know, "Downhearted Blues," my record for Paramount, was the first blues ever to sell 100 percent mechanical. They were on every phonograph label, and that's
what I told you to remind me of the player pianos, because Pete Wendel and Max Cortlander had the piano rolls with "Downhearted Blues" on it.
Yes.
See?
Did you get money out of piano rolls?
Yes.
You did.
Uh-huh.
They paid you for that.
Yeah. Yeah. And in the meantime, let me see now, there was something else I wanted to tell you. Piano rolls, Max Cortlander, and something -- wait now, let me see what it was, what it was.
Do you want to stop for a minute?
